Udyog Manager

Product idea and launch plan

A billing and business management platform for merchants, with planned web, mobile and chatbot access. One credit per finalized bill, priced at ₹1.

Prepared for the founder, prospective collaborators and development partners. This document explains the idea, planned experience, commercial model and delivery priorities. Technical proposals and unapproved policies are identified as such.

1 The idea

Udyog Manager is a proposed billing and business management product for merchants. Its purpose is to bring bills, customer history, payment collections, outstanding dues, purchases and expenses into one dependable record. The product will be accessible through a web application, a mobile application and a conversational assistant.

The founder has purchased udyogmanager.com. The product is currently described as in development; no customer traction, release date or completed capabilities are claimed. The target audience spans merchant categories, with specialized workflows delivered in stages.

2 The customer problem

A merchant needs to know what was sold, what money arrived, who still owes money and what the business spent. When these records are scattered, everyday follow-up and accountant handoff become harder. These are product hypotheses to validate with interviews and a pilot, rather than quantified market-research findings.

The intended experience is simple enough for daily counter use while preserving accurate records underneath. A quick bill should not come at the cost of unreliable balances or duplicated transactions.

3 Product scope

The shared foundation includes business onboarding, customers and suppliers, products and services, invoice drafts, finalized bills, PDF sharing, payment recording, outstanding balances, purchases, expenses, credits and reports. Goods businesses also need stock movements and an appropriate costing method to support meaningful profit reports.

Retail and service workflows can establish the common base. Wholesale price lists, restaurant kitchen orders, pharmacy batches and expiry dates, repair job cards and manufacturing workflows each need dedicated requirements and validation. The long-term all-category vision should not be advertised as complete day-one specialist coverage.

4 The merchant journey

A merchant creates a business profile, selects the business category, enters relevant tax details, adds items or services, and recharges credits. They prepare a bill, review totals and confirm issuance. The system assigns an invoice number, consumes one credit and saves the financial record. The merchant can then share the bill and record full or partial payment.

Later payments reduce the outstanding balance. Returns, corrections and refunds remain traceable to their original records. Reprinting a bill does not issue another invoice or charge another credit. At month end, the merchant or accountant reviews registers and exports supporting information.

5 Commercial model

The confirmed pricing unit is ₹1 per generated bill through credits. The proposed operational definition is one successfully finalized bill, with an official invoice number. Adding customers is free. Drafts, repeat downloads and payment updates should not consume bill credits.

Merchants buy credit packages instead of making a separate online payment for every ₹1 charge. Suggested package sizes can be tested during the pilot. The founder still needs to approve tax-inclusive or tax-exclusive presentation, minimum recharge, promotional credits, expiry, cancellation treatment and refunds. The welcome page therefore identifies the price as planned and does not take payments.

Existing records and exports should remain accessible at zero credits. New chargeable issuance can be blocked with a clear recharge prompt, while payment recording and draft preparation remain available.

6 Business and accountant reports

The dashboard should separate net sales, collections, receivables, expenses and profit. Collections are not the same as revenue. Profit needs complete cost and expense information, including inventory costing when goods are sold. Missing information should be clearly flagged instead of presenting a partial result as final profit.

Plan sales and purchase registers, customer statements, expense summaries, tax-component summaries and accountant-readable exports. GST preparation and reconciliation require current-rule validation by a practicing CA. The first release prepares records for review; direct filing and external fiscal integrations are separate milestones.

The detailed product specification contains the accounting examples, proposed GST workflows and official references. Those references and applicable rules should be rechecked during implementation rather than treating this concept document as a tax opinion.

7 Web mobile and chatbot

The web experience provides a full dashboard and efficient record management. The mobile app supports daily billing, customer lookup and sharing. The chatbot helps answer questions such as “Who has unpaid bills?” and can prepare a structured bill draft.

All three channels must use the same backend rules. Financial actions through chat require a preview and merchant confirmation. The model should not independently calculate taxes or directly edit financial tables. A failure in the AI service must not prevent normal web or mobile billing.

Online bill finalization is the proposed initial design. Fully offline issuance needs a deliberate plan for numbering, reserved credits and conflict resolution; it should not be promised until implemented.

8 Technology direction

The confirmed stack is Django for the core backend, Next.js for the web frontend and FastAPI for the chatbot service. React Native with Expo is the proposed mobile choice, with PostgreSQL as the authoritative database. Background jobs generate PDFs, exports and notifications.

Django owns tenant permissions, invoice calculations, credit deductions and accounting operations. FastAPI orchestrates conversational requests through authorized Django APIs. The initial backend can be a modular application with explicit business-service boundaries rather than many independently deployed services.

A bill and its credit deduction must commit together. Duplicate requests must return the same saved result. Recharge credits are granted only after server-side payment verification, with duplicate provider events prevented from granting credits twice.

9 Trust and operational readiness

Every business record, export and file download needs server-side access checks. Staff and accountant roles should expose only the information each person needs. Financial corrections need an audit trail. Sensitive data should be minimized in logs and protected in storage and transit.

Before paid launch, test concurrent credit deductions, failed PDFs, repeated recharge webhooks, partial-payment reversals, cross-business access attempts and backup restoration. These are planned engineering requirements, not assertions of completed audits or certifications.

10 Pilot and delivery

Begin with discovery across several merchant categories and a CA review. Build the common onboarding, billing, credit and payment flows; add purchases, expenses and supporting reports; then test them with real pilot merchants. Mobile and a bounded chatbot can reuse those proven APIs.

A useful pilot measures time to first bill, successful issuance, repeat usage, recharge conversion, report completeness and support effort. Introduce specialist modules based on observed needs. Dates and budget should be estimated after team capacity and first-release scope are agreed.

11 Illustrative economics

At 100 active merchants issuing 300 chargeable bills each month, the arithmetic usage value is 100 × 300 × ₹1 = ₹30,000 per month. At 500 merchants with the same use, it is ₹150,000. These figures are scenarios, not forecasts or evidence of demand.

Payment processing, hosting, storage, support and AI usage reduce contribution. Taxes, refunds and promotional credits also affect results. Recharge cash receipts can differ from credits consumed and revenue recognized during a period. Unit economics need real pilot data before scaling.

12 Brand and welcome page

The brand uses deep green, warm ivory and a light green accent. The icon combines a U with ledger lines to represent organized business records. The supporting message is “Your bills. Your customers. Your business, in view.”

The welcome page is a lightweight static site for udyogmanager.com. It introduces the concept, planned channels and ₹1-per-bill model, and clearly says “Coming soon.” It does not collect personal information, take payments or claim the application is live. The supplied files can be uploaded to a static host and connected to the purchased domain.

13 Decisions and next steps

Approve the pricing and refund terms, first-release category workflows, supported languages, mobile release order and offline requirements. Recruit pilot merchants and an accounting adviser. Turn the detailed specification into an implementation backlog and validate the complete bill-to-payment journey.

For the domain, select hosting and obtain its exact DNS records before making changes. Preserve existing mail records. Publish the welcome page only after checking the production URL and HTTPS. The domain purchase alone does not establish website hosting.
